newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-RIOS CONTINUES TO WIN UGLY.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-RIOS CONTINUES TO WIN UGLY.

text.p: Marcelo Rios, the brooding artist of tennis, seldom looks like he enjoys himself on court.
On Tuesday the surly Chilean at least had reason for his sour mood after unheralded qualifier Wayne Black forced him to five sets in his opening match at the French Open.
Rios, the seventh seed, rode into Paris labelled as a dark horse to claim the French crown but that assessment may have as much to do with his dour moods as his ability to lift a grand slam title.
If Rios looked unhappy on court, attending his post-match press conference was about as fun as someone pulling his fingernails out.
"My goal is to win here and this year I have a chance," stated Rios flatly, after eventually showing up two hours late.

Never at ease with the press, Rios is not yet able to field questions with the same precision he handles serves, which might explain why he has been awarded the "Prix Citron" as the most unco-operative player on the men's circuit for the second consecutive year by tennis writers.
Even questions wrapped in a compliments prompt stinging returns.
When asked if he trains to prepare for five-set matches, Rios snapped back:
"You don't work and train to win the fifth set. "You train to win every set."
On another brilliant Parisian day, Rios spent much of his three hours on court skulking around the red clay as if a dark cloud were hanging over his head.
As usual, if there was, it was largely his own doing.

Black, the fifth lowest ranked player in the men's field at 250 and playing at Roland Garros for the first time on a surface he claims to be his least favourite, gave the pony-tailed Chilean a rough ride.
As the contest progressed, so did Rios' scowls and racket throwing.
In close matches Rios is often his own worse enemy and there are those who claim that when the going gets tough, Rios just leaves.
He appeared on his way out against Black until the fourth game of the fourth set when he broke the Zimbabwean to take a 3-1 lead and went on to win 10 of the next 11 games.
"I thought he was getting ready to pack it in at the end of the second and start of the third," said Black. "But I knew this was a grand slam so he wasn't going to give it away completely.
"Maybe he would have at any another tournament."
A winner in Monte Carlo and a finalist in Rome, Rios' play this season had many not only touting him as the potential French Open champion but as the successor to the 'King of Clay', Thomas Muster.
But that crown may yet go to someone else with 'the King' and his heir apparent barely surviving five-set tests in the first round of the $10 million tournament.
